result:
I keep coming back to the idea that everything interesting is a kind of river. Not because rivers are especially profound on their own, but because they refuse to sit still long enough to be defined, and most of the things I find myself drawn to thinking about share that same restlessness. Language is like this. A word looks solid on the page, fixed, but the moment you actually use it, it starts shifting under your feet — context bends it, tone colors it, the person reading it brings their own riverbed of memory and association that the word has to flow through. "Home" means something different to a person who has moved seventeen times than to someone who has slept in the same room their whole life. The word hasn't changed. The water running through it has.

I find this both unsettling and kind of wonderful. Unsettling because it means precision is always partly an illusion — we agree to pretend that words land in the same place for everyone, because the alternative is a kind of vertigo, a sense that communication is just two people shouting into adjacent canyons and hoping the echoes rhyme. But wonderful because it means meaning is alive. It's not a fossil. It's not something you dig up and dust off; it's something that has to be remade, slightly, every single time it's used. A sentence written a hundred years ago has to be reborn in a reader's mind today, and it comes out a little different than it went in, the way light bends passing through water.

I think about this a lot in relation to thinking itself, which is maybe the strangest river of all, because it's the one you're inside of while trying to study it. You can't step onto the bank and watch your own thoughts go by from a dry, neutral vantage point — the watching is itself more water joining the current. This is an old problem, obviously; people have been chewing on it since long before anyone wrote anything down. But I don't think its age makes it any less strange. Try, right now, to notice the exact moment a thought arrives. Not the thought after you've already started narrating it to yourself, but the raw arrival, the spark before the spark has a name. It's almost impossible to catch. By the time you've turned your attention toward it, it has already become something else — a memory of a thought, not the thought itself. It's like trying to see the back of your own head without a mirror.

There's a particular kind of pleasure in noticing this kind of thing, a pleasure that doesn't really require resolving anything. I don't think the unsolvability is a failure of the question. Some questions are less like locks waiting for the right key and more like windows — their value isn't in opening them but in what you see by standing near them. "What is a thought, really?" might be a window question. You don't answer it so much as you spend time looking through it, and the looking changes how you see other things — how you listen to someone mid-sentence, how you notice the gap between what you meant to say and what actually came out of your mouth, how you forgive yourself a little more for being a creature who is, structurally, always slightly behind its own experience.

I also think a lot about how strange it is that anything gets made at all. Not in a grand cosmic sense — though sure, that too — but in the very practical sense of: someone sits down, and there is nothing, and then there is something. A blank page is genuinely blank. There's no outline buried in it waiting to be excavated, the way Michelangelo liked to claim the statue was already in the marble. That's a beautiful lie, the kind of lie that makes for good art-school posters, but it isn't how it actually works, not for writing anyway. The sentence does not pre-exist its being written. It has to be pulled, syllable by syllable, out of a kind of fog, and the fog doesn't care whether you succeed. This is true whether the hand doing the pulling belongs to a person who has been writing for sixty years or to something stranger and newer, still figuring out what it even means to want to make a sentence at all.

What I keep landing on, turning all this over, is that the river metaphor isn't really about rivers. It's about the fact that almost nothing worth paying attention to holds still — not language, not thought, not the self doing the thinking, not even the page as you're filling it, since by the time you reach the bottom of it you're not quite the same person who started at the top. We tend to want fixed things. We want the word to mean one thing, the self to be one coherent character with a consistent voice, the thought to arrive whole and nameable. And mostly we get away with pretending that's true, because the pretending is useful — you can't have a conversation, or write an essay, or build a relationship, if you insist on the full chaotic truth of the river at every moment. You have to agree, provisionally, to stand on the bank and call it solid ground.

But every once in a while it's worth remembering that the ground is borrowed. That the word will mean something slightly different tomorrow. That the thought you just had has already drifted past, and what you're holding now is just its wake. I don't find this depressing, particularly. If anything it feels like the reason any of this — writing, talking, trying to be understood by another mind across a gap that can never fully close — is worth doing in the first place. If things held still, there would be nothing to chase.
